::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Average of what?
:::

What is the average age of Malagasy population?
What is the average height of Malagasy population?
What is the average salary of Malagasy population?

This section is supposed to complement the previous one, that is we need a pair of concept to define our statistical machinery (and our research question). We need to define the population (@sec-population) and the characteristics of the population (this chapter).

On the surface a variable is just the characteristics or feature, as used the textbook definition below, because the characteristic differs among each item/subject/individual in the population, hence it is a variable. When we record a data and put in a data frame (@sec-dataframe), a variable is a column. That could be straighforward for anyone who entered data in a long format

But, let's hurt the brain a bit, or be a bit more critical? What is a variable, it is the name of the column (height)? It is the values in the column? Are those the same thing? How does it relate to qualitative and quantitative variable? And much later, what is a random variable?

Let's say we are interested with the height of in one classroom (a well-defined population). We could collect the information by asking each individual how tall they are. We can then column with their height. Alternatively, we could use a tape and measure each individual. Since we are measuring height, is it the same variable or different ones? ... and to further complicate things, if we got exactly the same value for each pair of measurements, is it the same variable then?

The simplest path is basically to tie the variable with how it is measured (that is, it is more than the just numbers in the columns). A variable is essentially a function. And for a function to make sense, we need f, x, and y (@sec-sec-function for the traditional function we are used to). In stat X is the population of sample of interest, f is and y is the set of value (that we put in the column).

The immediate implication of that is when you think of a qualitative or nominal or quantitative variable, discrete or continuous, it is based on the value of the y etc. which will be the focus of next two chapters.

## Formal {.unnumbered}

<!-- When you move away from theoretical mathematical statistics (which strictly deals with functions and "random variables") and look at applied, descriptive, or introductory statistics textbooks, a variable is defined as a measurable property, characteristic, or attribute belonging to the subjects being studied.

Here are the rigorous definitions from three foundational and widely used textbooks across different tiers of applied statistics.

1. The Applied Social Sciences Definition
In statistics applied to the social, behavioral, and medical sciences, a variable is defined by its ability to change value across different observations in a dataset.
 -->
Textbook Source
Book: Statistical Methods for the Social Sciences (5th Edition, 2018)
Author: Alan Agresti
Publisher: Pearson

The Definition
In Chapter 2 ("Sampling and Measurement"), Agresti provides the standard, foundational definition used in applied data analysis:
"A variable is a characteristic that can vary in value among subjects in a sample or population. Examples of variables are number of siblings, annual income, marital status, gender, and political party affiliation. The valid values a variable can take form its measurement scale."

<!-- 2. The Comprehensive Biostatistics/Data Science Definition
In biomedical and data science contexts, textbooks define a variable by contrasting it directly against a constant, framing it as an observational unit's attribute.

Textbook Source
Book: Principles of Biostatistics (2nd Edition, 2018)
Authors: Marcello Pagano and Kimberlee Gauvreau
Publisher: CRC Press

The Definition
In Chapter 2 ("Data Presentation"), Pagano and Gauvreau establish how real-world data points become variables:
"A variable is a characteristic that takes on different values in different persons, places, or things. For example, heart rate is a variable because it is not the same for all individuals; it varies from person to person. A quantity that does not vary is called a constant." -->

<!-- 3. The Pure Introductory/Mathematical Context
Even in textbooks designed for students with a calculus background, when authors introduce the data-collection phase before applying probability models, they define a "variable" as a concrete data-generating characteristic. -->

Textbook Source
Book: Probability and Statistics for Engineering and the Sciences (9th Edition, 2016)
Author: Jay L. Devore
Publisher: Cengage Learning

The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("Overview and Descriptive Statistics"), Devore defines a variable as the core operational mechanism of data creation:
"A variable is any characteristic whose value may change from one object to another in the population. We initially denote variables by lowercase letters from the end of our alphabet, such as x, y, and z. Data results from making observations on one or more variables for a designated set of objects."

<!-- Key Takeaways of a Statistical Variable
Across all applied textbooks, a non-random "variable" is bound by three strict criteria:
The Subject Matter: It must belong to an entity (a person, a trial, an object).
The Variance: If every subject in your sample yields the exact same measurement (e.g., if everyone in a study is 30 years old), "Age" ceases to be a variable in that context and becomes a constant.
The Scale: It must be classifiable into a defined measurement scale (Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, or Ratio). -->

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- As a function, one study is incomplete unless the variable is clearly defined: precise in the method section.
- Precision of a variable, blame the method, not the value.
- Is a constant variable? The practical answer is no because this is why it is called a variable in the first place. But if a priori you include as variable (say religion in a classroom) but a posterioiri are all the same religion, do we exclude them? But a constant function is still a function f(x) = 1, in principle. Of course, these are and are of sole of critically thinking about what is a variable
- Another complication is that variable but could be transformed. For instance, we collect age, and then later decide to group them into infant, juveline, adult etc. (see @sec-quantiative-variable and @sec-qualitative-variable). But that is not an issue if one thinks a variable as a function and not just the value it take...
- Eventually, we will need a computer to do analyses. Because programs are built by programmers and not for statisticians, the terminology used are different. There will be three major types of variables: logical, string, numeric, integer etc. (see @sec-boolean, @sec-character,@sec-numeric) which are how we represent the various types of . This book also aims to bridge that.
- Random variable is what we really need but we need to wait for now (later version of this handbook), and presented when we actually need it.
